Tim had reached out over the weekend that the chiller had shut down again, and asked if I could check it out Monday morning. I arrived on site, and immediately went to the chiller, found chiller left in alarm for Evap pressure low in both circuits 1 and 2. After doing a preliminary check, I reset the alarms and begun to watch as the chiller came online. Whilst tracking circuit #2 data, I found LWT (Leaving Water Temperature) was reading 148°, and EWT (Entering Water Temperature) was reading 68°. I immediately knew the sensor was inaccurate, and likely causing the low pressure alarms, as the chiller was bringing on all stages of cooling trying to reach an unreachable setpoint. Causing each circuit to run until tripping on low pressure. I begun to disassemble side panels to access the failed water temperature sensor, removed, and spliced in a new universal sensor I had on my van. Once I checked the new reading I noticed it was reading even higher (194°), I begun ohming out new sensor, and found it was 960ohms, after tracking the correct chart, I found the sensors i had on my van were not 10k ohm which is what was needed for the Microtech III controller. I bypassed the spliced water temperature sensor cable, and took existing daikin sensor and wired it into the Microtech III, after performing a power reset. I now found Original sensor reading ~55° which was OAT, and accurate. Unsure if the cable was the issue or not, I took the original sensor, and wired it back into the cable, and re-installed into the temperature well, and found sensor again was reading correctly. (~52°)Reset chiller to begun running and taking the load over. I continued to watch the chiller operate without any issues, staging, and cycling as needed without any problems. After speaking with Tim I explained that we had a potential sensor issue, or possibly an intermittent Microtech controller issue. I asked Tim if he was okay with me installing a new sensor to eliminate the possibility of a faulty sensor. He approved, so I was able to contact Rick, and he was able to grab a new daikin sensor from our parts department. Once I had the new sensor, I begun removing existing sensor, and ran new cable and tied into correct terminals. Reset chiller, and found sensor reading correctly. Observed chillers operation, to ensure there were no other issues. We will need to watch chillers operation, if the chiller proceeds to go into alarm it is likely we have a failing Microtech III controller. Tim is aware of the plan, and approved. Tim will reach out if/when the chiller goes into alarm again. Please use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/9ABD7964-9D0A-4466-88F1-D3EF01BA23F8

Task: replace condensate pump on first floor, speak with Derik about central controller not matching roomsSummary : Condensate pump - I located in FCU’s that had a faulty condensing pumpVerify, there was no condensate in the drain Removed the condensate pump and installed new condensate pump Poured water into the drain pan and watched condensate get pumped out Central controller and system operation:Met with Derik at the central controllerHe was having an issue, sending a command via the UI He would send a call to all the units to run at 65° to verify they were all cooling, however, the unit would quickly revert back to either off or a different desired temperature.There’s only occurred with the unit using the thermostat adapter .Investigated and found the following .The central controller does not have control over the FCU’s  when the thermostatic adapter is set to be controlled off the thermostatThe central controller reads the return air temperature from the FCU’s The 3rd part stats send a 24v call to y1, y2, w1,or w2 in thethermostat adapter based on the requested temperature at the 3rd party statEach terminal has a predetermined desired temp value Ex. 24v callY1=desired temp 72°FY2= desired temp, 68°FW1= desired temp, 72°FW2= desired temp, 77°FThis desired temp is then sent as a command to the FCUWhen the third party start satisfies, the unit is turned off until a new call is present.Please use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/B31E5534-B6A0-40BE-93C4-0AAD50808741

Task: investigate hp 53 tripping on high head pressure.SummaryMet with Luke onsite and gained access to the heat pump. The unit has tripped on the high pressure alarm inconsistently.I turned the water off and inspected the strainer. The strainer was clean and was not restricted. Verified water flow. Checked evaporator coilfor buildup.  Checked fan for operation. Cycled system in heat and allowed units to run. Incoming water temperature was 65 degrees leaving was 53. Superheat on both stages was 12. Subcool was 15. Amped the fan motor at 2/3 Amps. Compressors averaged an amperage of 7A.Stage one heat had a discharge air temperature of 89. With second stage running discharge temperature was 112. Room made setpoint within 15 minutes. Circuit one had a head pressure of 380 circuit 2 had a head pressure of 390. Ran the cooling mode and had a discharge air temperature of 41. When the room temperature was cooled to 66 we reengaged the heat and set it for 77. Observed the pressures of the system during an abnormally long runtime and an over heated space. The pressures remained stable until the return air temperature rise above 72. The head pressure began to spike and nearly hit 500psi. This is a high pressure.  The system is equipped with Merv 13 filters and has a higher air restriction then the original Merv 8. We cooled the space down and removed the filters. Repeated the long runtime test and the head pressure stabilized at 420 even when the return temperature rose above 72. The observation leads to the conclusion that the filters are restricting air and the unit is unable to remove enough heat when the space  temperature is warm. Verified air supply to the unit. The system is running and operational. Spoke with Dylan, and Melissa to gain information regarding the history of this job. It was made aware to me the recently replaced flow switch was not working properly. Once I received a picture of the current flow switch (Differential Pressure) I found the current switch was not the proper switch, so I was able to locate the correct differential pressure switch, and all materials needed to install it. I proceeded to head to the job site, once on-site I was able to make contact with willie, to gain access to the mechanical room where I located (1) Trane Chiller;M#: RTWD110FS#: U14J00119Chiller was running upon initial arrival, I begun inspecting inlet and outlet water pressure of evaporator side, found ~65psi entering, ~64psi leaving. Found 57° entering chilled water, and 43° leaving chilled water, thus indicating a lack of water flow through the evaporator. I begun tracing piping, and identifying valves were in their proper position, however the bypass valve was extremely hard to access. I called Dylan to check on our controls side as I was curious of the building differential pressure setpoint, and actual reading. Upon speaking with Dylan, he found the building differential was 38psi, and the setpoint was 15psi. He also found the bypass valve was 100% closed. I questioned why the bypass valve was closed, as he begun investigating the programming of the building bypass valve, he found the valve was programmed backwards. It was set up as reverse acting, when it needed to be direct acting. So when the building differential increased due to lack of load in the building, the valve begun to shut, when it actually needed to open to allow proper flow through the evaporator barrel on the chiller. Once Dylan corrected the programming issue, I immediately found an increase in differential pressure across the evaporator, and a huge reduction of temperature split across the evaporator. I then proceeded to check the previously installed Paddle flow switch, after making proper spring adjustments I was able to confirm the chiller closes flow switch upon flow, and opens flow switch upon the building pump stopping. I now had to remove the wiring from the incorrect differential pressure switch last installed, and run wiring back to the new paddle switch. Once it was all wired correctly I was able to confirm proper flow. Checked out with willie and explained my findings and what work I performed. Job complete. Note: All material purchased for this job was not used, I will return all materials. Please use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/30BCF98F-5701-4162-B973-BBAB27EF4928

SAARC Rtu 6 Low Oil Pressure Alarm 3/24/23Jacob ERtu 6 Low Oil Pressure AlarmArrived onsite with Keith, Havtech Technician, and checked in with Jackson, PG Utilities. Received access to Rtu 6 and unit was in alarm for low oil pressure for circuit 1 and 2. Checked both circuits oil site glasses on compressors and both were full. Cleared the alarms on the control touchpad and had Jackson call the controls technician to lower setpoint for unit to come on in A/C mode. Once setpoints were changed, compressor 1 came on and ran. Observed operation and noticed the suction pressure dropped to 90psig and discharge pressure was fluctuating from 305psig-400psig. As the discharge pressure would rise, the oil in the site glass would come down and go into a warning and then would go into alarm and turn the compressor off after about 5 minutes of running. Checked to make sure all water valves were in the proper position. Made sure the proper dampers were open. Cleared the alarm for circuit 1 and compressor 1 came on and ran. After 5 minutes, the compressor went into alarm again for low oil pressure and the site glass was almost empty of oil. Hooked up temperature probes and gauges across the liquid line solenoid valve and filter drier. Cleared alarm for circuit 1 and compressor 1 came on and ran. Found there wasn’t a temperature difference across the filter drier, so we hooked up temperature probes on both sides of the solenoid valve. Found a temperature difference across the liquid line solenoid valve for circuit 1. When there is a temperature difference across the solenoid valve, there is either a faulty valve or the solenoid coil isn’t being energized properly. We forced the unit off and turned power off to unit. Unhooked the liquid line solenoid coil and put a magnet on the valve body to see if the magnet would pull the valve open to allow refrigerant to pass through valve. Turned power on to unit and observed operation. Circuit 1 came on and we monitored pressures and temperatures across the liquid line solenoid valve. The solenoid valve is supposed to be open during unit operation and it was only opening half way allowing minimum refrigerant to pass through the valve causing the suction pressure to drop and losing the oil out of the compressor. We documented the temperature across the liquid line solenoid valve for circuit 1 during operation. Unit will need a new liquid line solenoid valve, solenoid coil, new filter drier cores, and new refrigerant. The pressures for circuit 1 look low and without having a proper liquid line solenoid valve operation, adding refrigerant to circuit 1 isn’t a good option at this time. With circuit 1 being in alarm, we began looking at circuit 2. Circuit 2 was also in alarm for low oil pressure upon arrival. We observed operation of circuit 2 once the compressor came on and ran. We tested circuit 2 in all operating modes, which include blower mode, Dehumidification, A/C, Space heat, and Pool Heat. We monitored temperatures and pressures and was not able to get circuit 2 to go into any oil pressure alarm. The only alarm that was generated for circuit 2 was low pressure alarm. That was generated by me opening the door of the unit in the evaporator section, which send the air out of the door way and not across the coil. That will bring the suction pressure down while in operation. We continued to monitor circuit 2 and it is running properly under normal operation with no alarms at this time. Circuit 1 is in alarm and will not run until alarm is cleared and the repair is made on the liquid line solenoid valve. We did find oil coming from the bottom fitting on the circuit 2 liquid line solenoid valve. I recommend replacing the solenoid valve, solenoid coil, and filter drier core for circuit 2. Also, I recommend putting new refrigerant back into circuit 2 once the new liquid line solenoid valve and filter drier cores are replaced. Once the refrigerant is recovered, there is a possibility the refrigerant charge recovered is lower than the factory charge for circuit 2 because of the leak on the liquid line solenoid valve bottom fitting. Communicated with Jackson and another PG Utilities worker on work that was performed and what was found. Cleaned up workspace and checked out. Job complete. **Quote Needed** Replacing Circuit 1 Liquid Line Solenoid Valve, Solenoid Coil, Core Drier for filter drier, and adding new refrigerant to Circuit 1. Repair Of Refrigerant Circuit On Rebel UnitSteve and I Upon trying to do start up on unit saw issues with Suction and Discharge from the Refrigerant Cycle.After verification of Transducers and Pressures on system we Decided the next best course of action with to Begin by pulling the charge and testing to see if there was a leak. As I began to get ready to Pull the charge I was looking for the best port to pull the charge from the system out, I felt a slick substance behind the port and when I pulled the removed the Loose cap from the port The schrader was full of oil and Bubbling out, I took the best Pictures possible of the oil and residue on the 1/4” port and tightened the schrader core back inEllis with Technical services also visually saw the oil and gas running out of the top as the cap was removed, it appears the Schrader push pin was turned out just high enough to allow it to slightly open the Valve in the schrader. I then tightened the port back up and began to remove the gas, At the point we’re I took my gauges off the unit I also noticed a hissing sound out of the Port coming right before the compressor on the suction side, and tightened that loose schrader as well. (At this point I went to every schrader core and checked all of them and verified all of them were tight and seated and not leaking) Gas removed was 11lbs 12.75oz’s I pulled the unit down to 10psi on the high side and 6.7psi on the low When I returned from gathering all the other Materials off my truck the pressure had no risen or fallen,At that point after discussing this with Steve we came to the determination to weigh the proper charge back into the system with great gas and finish the start up process. We then charged the system Back Up with fresh 410a As instructed 18lbs 2oz as the Name plate indicated and then Finished start up Process. Pressures improved tremendously from original Beginning Suction 46.2psiAfter Repair 101-88psiUnit is Functional and Is not into alarm.Was discharging 52° air upon departure.Completed Yes:Materials used:Recovery bottleRecovery machine Gauges Basic hand tools18lbs. 2oz of 410aPlease use the following URL to FEASIBILITY STUDYSOLUTION(S)Recommendations The following recommendations are fairly straight-forward and based on improving the operation of the existing equipment.  Additional system efficiency upgrade recommendations, which require more significant system modifications, are included further below.   1.	The control sequences for all equipment should be reviewed and verified for applicability and most energy efficient operation.  Once all control modifications have been completed a retro-commissioning effort should be implemented to confirm the HVAC equipment operates in accordance with the design intent. 2.	In order to limit the number of air handling units operating to satisfy the lab spaces, detailed load calculations should be performed for the building.   If it appears the loads should be sustainable with only one air handling unit, the control sequences should be confirmed to make sure the systems are operating correctly.  If the calculated cooling loads slightly exceed the capacity of one air handling unit, the chilled water temperatures should be adjusted to provide additional capacity at the same airflow.  Based on the TAB reports provided to us, it appears the fans in AHU's 1, 2  3 are maxed out at approximately 20,000cfm of airflow and 4.8-inches of total static pressure. 3.	All paired pump installations should be checked to ensure check valves are installed on the discharge of each pump.  There is a significant waste of energy when a pump is run just to offset the back pressure of a paired pump. 4.	With regards to the high space temperatures in the labs, it is believed the space temperatures will be better controlled once the building controls are retro commissioned. 5.	Variable frequency drives should be installed on the hot water pre-heat pumps, as well as two-way control valves at the pre-heat coils, to allow the flow to adjust based on a set pre-heat coil discharge temperature, providing pump energy savings as the outdoor air temperatures increase. 6.	As the existing chillers already require replacement, and the customer wants to utilize chillers for cooling, it is recommended new air-cooled chillers be provided more closely matching the required building load.  Three smaller chillers, or replacement of the chillers with DX/furnace or heat pump AHU's, should be provided with one being stand-by for system redundancy.  A water-cooled chiller, with dual compressors, could also be considered if there is concern related to the installation of the new air-cooled chillers in the available space.  A water-cooled chiller will require the installation of a cooling tower and associated pumps. 7.	If chillers/boilers are used, the steam boilers should be replaced with modular hot water boilers, eliminating the need for steam to hot water converters.  Although, the pre-heat piping loop should still have a converter so that glycol can be provided in the system to avoid frozen coils.  An alternative would be to provide a separate boiler(s) for the pre-heat piping system, allowing direct use of glycol.  Other System Efficiency Upgrade Recommendations As mentioned previously, the following system efficiency upgrade recommendations involve significant modifications to the existing building systems.  However, the utility cost savings may justify the cost to implement the changes.  8.	If chillers are chosen, convert the existing primary-secondary chilled water system to a variable primary chilled water system.  This option would allow simplification of the current chilled water pumping arrangement, reducing the number of chilled water pumps from seven to three.  This would provide efficiencies in system operation, as well as reduced maintenance costs associated with the pumps.  New two-way valves would be required at the chilled water coils, as well as system controls modifications.  Redundancy would be provided by the installation of the three pumps, each sized for 50% off the required flow. 9.	Provide a run-around heat recovery piping system to capture heat from the air exhausted from the building and utilize it to preheat the hot water pre-heat water, prior to adding heat at the steam to hot water converters.  Coils would be required in the exhaust air ducts with piping connecting the new coils to the existing hot water pre-heat loop.  It is possible the existing hot water pre-heat pumps would need to be replaced to accommodate the flow rate and additional pressure drop of the new coils. 10.	Implement a night setback in the controls system, reducing the air changes in the labs which currently receive 9-11 air changes per hour, to half that during unoccupied hours.  All tenant and building occupants would need to be aware of the change in system operation.  Tenants would also have to be provided with a means to over-ride the system, placing their lab in occupied operation should they work during the scheduled unoccupied hours. 11.	Item 10 above can be improved by adding occupancy sensors in each lab which control the air changes in each lab; however, this increases complexity and cost to the lab control system.    12.	An alternative to replacing chillers and boilers is to replace the existing AHU's with AHU's with DX cooling and gas furnaces.  This option will eliminate the need for chillers and boilers.  The sensible heat for the lab spaces will be handled by the addition of a Variable Refrigerant Volume (VRV) system.  This VRV system would have water-cooled condensing units that would take advantage of the heat recovery loop.  This option would allow for decreased maintenance, the elimination of chilled water pumps, higher efficiencies and better system control.  THE THREE POTENTIAL SOLUTIONS ARE OUTLINED BELOW:Solution 1 (Baseline)Replace existing 270-ton chillers only1. Arrived onsite, and gained access to lobby area. Spoke to security to get in contact with VA4 OPS personnel. They were able to contact Nick, and he was able to give me access to the rooftop where I located;AaonM#: RN-030-3-0-E70A-000S#: 201904-BNCT15760Found circuit #1 tripped, and circuit #2 running. Reset circuit #1 found circuit tripped again shortly after starting, upon further diagnosis I found the circuit pumping down whilst loaded. I begun investigating possible restrictions within the circuit. Found Liquid line filter drier had a 40° split across it, thus causing the suction side of the system to pump down and tripping low pressure switch causing the circuit lockout. I spoke with my escort nick, and made him aware the filter drier was the issue, he contacted Ben and gave me the go ahead to begin repairs. I headed back down to my van to grab all necessary tools and materials to begun Refrigerant recovery. Once back to the roof, I shut down, and tagged out the unit. I begun refrigerant recovery of circuit #1. Circuit holds 24lbs of R-410A, i recovered 23lbs. Once refrigerant was removed I begun coming up with a game plan to replace filter drier as it was in hard to access area of the compressor section. I decided I was going to coupling the inlet side of the drier, however I did not have 5/8” couplings on my van. Headed to supply house to pick up couplings, nitrogen, a new bottle of 410A, and replacement schraders. Begun the removal of the clogged filter drier, then fitting new one in place. Once new filter drier was brazed in, I begun a pressure test @ 200psi to check for immediate leaks. With none found, I pumped system up to 400psi, to be left overnight for a pressure hold test. Disabled circuit #1 @ low pressure switch, and pulled compressor fuses, then started unit back up to allow circuit #2 to provide cooling overnight. Cleaned up tools and debris. Will return tomorrow to continue on the repairs.  Checked out with Ben. Job is ongoing.

Arrived on site, Unit still leaking after test run.After further investigation on site last week we Previously addressed in an email the Condensate Drain Trap was not proper. And did not go by Manufacturer reccomendations.The vent on the trap is Not Per Manufacturer Specification nor is the height and drop of the trap.Install Manual States. “Condensate drain stub is .75 O D.. Drain lines and traps should run full size from the drain pan stub. Drain pans should have traps to allow condensate from coils to drain freely. The trap depth and distance between the trap outlet and the drain pan outlet should be twice the static pressure in the drain pan section under normal operation for the trap to remain sealed.” Static pressure at unit is -0.62incwMike Roemer, decided to cap the vent on the begging side of the trap, And does not want to change the trap location we’re he could have more drop for the trap to make it proper Height per Manufacturer recommendations, Currently the trap measurement from start of the trap pipe bottom to Leaving the trap pipe bottom is less than 1/4” difference, Manufacture statement says that with the static at a -0.62 the from bottom pipe entering to bottom pipe exiting should be 1.24” Installing contractor is going to leave trap as is and cap the Vent and Check it periodically through to the day to verify the unit doesn’t overflow. CompletedMaterials Used Basic Hand tools.Please use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/237A5EEE-3610-470F-AEA5-2BB6D7619374

Arrived on site and met with Tommy, Tommy contacted security to give us access to the school. Once security arrived, we were able to gain access to the school, all mechanical rooms, and rooftop. Upon arrival we located Daikin Chiller;M#: AGZ241ETSEPNN0AS#: STNU210700168We checked active, and history alarms on chiller upon first inspection, found a long list of Evaporator flow loss alarms. However upon inspection, we found electronic flow meter reading 100% flow. We shut chiller down, and located closest water connection to begun connecting hoses to reach the chiller for condenser coil cleaning. Once we had enough hose to reach the chiller, we gathered remaining needed tools to begun on the maintenance. Removed necessary covers to gain access to the condenser coils.Found condenser coils with a solid film of dirt on most of the coils. We worked as a team to begun washing down all condenser coils, ensuring all debris was being wash off the chiller at the same time. Once we were done with condenser coil cleaning, we restored power to the chiller, to allow the crankcase heaters operate overnight to be checked in the morning. Whilst cleaning up all tools, and hoses, we found the chiller came on and begun to run. As I went over to inspect chiller readings, I found the chiller shut off before I was able to get any readings. Found chiller shutdown on evaporator flow loss. Upon investigation, we found electronic flow meter was not measuring any flow through chiller evaporator. Once confirming pumps were still running, I begun going through Microtech controller in which I found Entering water temperature, and leaving water temperatures were reading 110°. We begun investigating potential issues, as the building is 4-pipe, there should be no way for the water to absorb that much heat. We checked a few thermometers at the AHU’s on the roof access level, and found they were also reading 110° CHW. We went down to the pump room, where we located the Chilled water pumps. Found (1) Pump running at 99%, 90psi discharge, 60psi suction. I removed suction strainer insulation cap to check for an estimate of water temperature at the pump, found suction strainer reading 110°. I then checked the temperature of the bearing assembly for the CHW pump that was running, and found bearing assembly at 145°. It appears we are potentially air locked in the pump volute, or in the CHW loop elsewhere. We have shut down the CHW pumps temporarily until we can return tomorrow to further investigate the issue. Job incomplete. Please use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/01FD67BD-8255-4F71-A878-46F338102C15

Arrived on site and met with Terry. Terry was able to give me access to the mechanical room. Upon arrival, I found Chiller #1 running, and maintaining load. After speaking with Terry he explained he started chiller #1 yesterday, and it was running okay since. However he explained Chiller #2 was surging real bad upon his initial start up. I begun investigating Chiller #2, as the purge should be removing any air accumulation during the winter months. I checked purge Pump out minutes/hours, and found none. I checked purge evaporator temperatures, and found they were not in the threshold to initiate a pump out. I decided to hook a gauge to the only access fitting on the purge compressor, and found the pressure reading was in a negative. I proceeded to isolate purge from the chiller using existing isolation valves, and isolated electrical to purge unit to ensure it would not power on the compressor. I grabbed nitrogen, and begun to pressurize the purge refrigeration side, pumped up to 150psi. I begun to leak check purge, and was unable to find any leaks. I then decided to check the chiller side that was now isolated. The condenser ball valve had a access fitting on the purge side, and upon checking, found all the nitrogen I had put into the purge side, had leaked over to the chiller side indicating a failed evaporator on the purge. This is non-repairable, and we will have to replace the purge before this chiller will be able to run. I then went over to Chiller #1 to get some readings as I had the suspicion the machine was low on refrigerant. Chiller was running @ ~40%FLABelow were my readings:Evap Pressure = 6psiaCond Pressure = 14.9psiaEvap Sat Temp = 41.5°Cond Sat Temp = 82.8°Discharge Temp = 118°Discharge Superheat = 35.5°Evap Approach = 3.5°Cond Approach = 1°Refrigerant Level = 11%Refrigerant level stpt = 20%The chiller does appear to be low on refrigerant as it was unable to make refrigerant level setpoint even with low load conditions, however unless this becomes and issue on higher load days, we will wait until repairs are made to correct the chiller charge. Gathered all information for the quote needed to replace Chiller #2 purge, I will provide all information needed. Cleaned up all tools, job is complete. Please use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/20110373-8CDF-46CA-91D1-4075C19D4479

Arrived on site and met with Mark. He explained the sanctuary intermittently gets warm. He was under the impression possibly a sensor was faulty. However he explained, every few days he would cycle power to the chiller and everything would start working again. He was unsure if the chiller was actually going into alarm or not though. Mark gave me keys and showed me the locations of the equipment, upon initial inspection I found the Trane Chiller;M#: CGAM052AS#: U11K25582Was in alarm for Evaporator flow loss, I checked alarm history and found a long list of evaporator flow loss alarms. I located Chilled water pump, and found it had no signal to run, later found the Trane system controls all these pieces of equipment. Enabled AHU by changing schedule, once AHU was enabled I found a signal for the Chilled water pump, and chiller was sent. Went back out to the chiller, reset alarm, and left chiller offline to check for possible flow switch issues. Found flow switch reading “no flow” with pump off, and “flow” with the pump running, leading me to believe the flow switch is operable. I then set chiller to auto, and headed back down to the Trane AHU. I begun observing operations, checking to ensure there was no signal issue to the chilled water pump, etc. Found system operating as expected. As the AHU begun to get closer to setpoint and 3-way valve begun to close, I checked valve to ensure it was operating properly with the system, whilst checking 3-way valve actuator I noticed one of the valves was ~90% closed, that valve is for the coil bypass, so when the 3-way valve starts to close, it diverts the water before entering the coil and sends it back to the system. With that valve being almost completely closed, when the AHU is close to satisfying and begun to shut down the cooling valve we are starving our pump of water, thus limited water flow through the chiller as there is no secondary bypass on this loop. I opened valve, and begun to stroke cooling valve open and closed, found no loss in water flow to the chiller. Whilst the system was running, I decided to check zone sensor accuracy, and found all sensors reading within a +/- 1° accuracy. Adjusted time schedule to allow system to shut down, checked on chiller, found chiller shut down properly with no alarms. Cleaned up all tools, and spoke with mark to explain my findings. Job complete. Please use the following URL to view Arrived on site and met with Butch. Butch explained Siemens was out last night to diagnose why Cooling Tower #1 would not operate. Butch explained Siemens stated, it was not a controls issue, and would have to be further diagnosed. Located Starter for CT-1, found in the off position upon arrival, I was able to access engineer computer to force CT-1 into enabled mode, fast speed. Upon my initial investigation I found no blown fuses, and the control transformer was operating properly. I begun to trace contactor coil wiring through the starter, and got lost at the Siemens panel. Butch was able to get me in contact with the Siemens tech that was on-site last night to let me know which relay on their controller was for this cooling tower as there was no diagram. Once I was able to identify the correct relay, I was able to confirm the Siemens controller was closed, thus suppose to be sending a signal to the starter to run in auto. However I found no voltage present at the Siemens controller, I then begun tracing the common 120v fed into the Siemens controller. Once I was able to identify the 120v feed came from the end switch on the cooling tower isolation valves, I went back to the computer to force open the valves. I found the end switch was still not closed, as I continued to troubleshoot, Butch wanted to temporarily turn on the chiller to bring the buildings down to temp. I explained to butch that I found the issue was a end switch for the cooling tower isolation valves, and butch gave me the approval to bypass the end switch to allow the cooling tower to function in auto mode. Once the end switch was bypassed, I found the 120v signal back to CT-1 starter, and was able to watch the fan start and run as expected. Dave was able to enable the rest of the CHW Plant, and I stayed to ensure a we had a problem-less start up. Once all other pumps came on and begun to run, we switched the chiller on, and it was able to start up and begun taking over the building load. Butch said he would get in touch with Siemens for the end switch, as they have just changed one of the isolation valves on CT-1. Chiller, and chilled water system in the main plant is now fully operational. Checked out with butch, job is complete. Please use the following URL to view related The tubes that had no flow prior to the tube brushing have some scale build up, but was minimal. The remaining tubes appear to be in good condition. Once all repairs were complete, we begun cleaning condenser end bell for re-installation. Wire Wheels both faces, and replaced with new gasket. Upon our leak test of the condenser end bell, we had a leak using the new gasket. We drained, and removed the end bell again to take a closer look. It appears the end bell face has been damaged, as it is missing chunks of material (see pics in XOI). Arrived on site and got access to the building and the roof. Fede showed me RTU-12 and explained to me that this past weekend they started having problems with the supply fan not running.I opened the blower service panel and found that the Schneider Electric VFD was in alarm EPH1 (loss of phase). Checked the voltage coming in to the unit and I had all 3 phases. I tightened all the electrical connections on the unit and the disconnect box attached to the unit. Reset power and while the unit was at Fan only mode and running at 30Hz system was operating normally, but when it got a call for heat and the blower speed got to 60Hz the vfd acted like it loss power for a quick second and start ramping up to 60Hz again. It will do this a bunch of times and then go into EPH1 alarm. Hooked meter at the bottom of the contactor where the power is coming in and noticed that PHASE B will drop voltage randomly.Met with Brian and Fede and explained what I found and recommended calling and electrician and have him check the breaker on the panel that feeds this unit and to check if there is a junction box between the panel and the unit. Brian called his Electrician and he said that the problem was at the unit and the VFD. Brian wanted me to check the unit again and I asked him if he approved for me to grab the VFD of a similar unit and install it on RTU-12 and he approved it.RTU-11 was the exact same unit and VFD. Removed the VFD from RTU-11 and install it on RTU-12.System was still going into alarm. I turned power to the unit and opened the disconnect built into the unit and as soon I opened one of the wires coming from the field installed disconnect box came loose. So I thought that was the problem. Reconnected the wire and tightened everything related to high voltage again. Restarted the unit and we still were dropping voltage on Phase B. Removed the Fuses inside of the disconnect box and install the fuses from another unit that had the same size and we still were dropping the voltage. I connected my electrical meter to the high voltage coming into the disconnect box and recorded a video showing how the voltage drops and it shows phase B dropping from 280VAC TO 120VAC.So that confirmed that the problem is the voltage feeding the unit.Met with Fede and explained to him what I found and showed him the video.They will call an electrician.Job is completePlease use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/E7AF29BF-4EA7-489C-88C2-46DFE2AEB4B6

I climbed into the unit through the outside air filter section to get access to the sensor. Made sure all the connections were tight. Cycled power to the unit and the sensors were still reading incorrectly. Went to my Van and got a 10K thermistor and hooked directly into the Envision controller Outside Air temp UI1-COM connections and the temperature reading was steady. I climbed into the unit again and wired the sensor. Checked the Envision controller and it was reading incorrectly again. I disconnected all the wires from the temperature/humidity sensor and wired the extra sensor to the black and white wires. Sensor was reading incorrectly. Wired the sensor to the blue and black wires and sensor was reading incorrectly again. I finally had to disconnect the 5vdc wire going to the outside temp/humidity sensor and wired the extra sensor that I had to blue and red wire and the sensor started reading correctly. The low voltage wiring between the Envision controller and Outside temperature/humidity sensor is damaged somewhere. I traced the wired as far as I could but didn’t find anything. I left the unit reading the outside temperature only that way it can cool the space.I recommend replacing the low voltage wiring between the Envision controller and Outside temp/hum sensor and also replace the Temp/hum sensor because we don’t know if the short caused damage to the sensor. I will create a XOI to send a repair quote to the customer.Work pendingPlease use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/E6C75F22-BAFC-4C18-99E8-F957F76043F5

Arrived on site and called POC Tyler (352) 213-8299. He contacted the building engineer so he can show me the Exhaust fan drive that needed to be started up.At first look the drive seemed that had a short because of the black smoke marks on the left side. Drive had power and confirmed that was getting the correct power. Drive had a 2021 alarm saying that start enable 1 was missing. Checked and programmed the parameters. I was still getting the same alarm. Checked the wiring and noticed that one of the wires was landed incorrectly and the safety interlock was not getting close. Fixed the wiring and alarm cleared.Building engineer came back with and electrician and the fire alarm technician so we can test the system. I set the drive on hand mode and the drive was sending power but motor did run and I will get an overcurrent alarm. With the VFD in off mode I was getting 19.5VAC between U2-V2, U2-W2 and 0VAC between V2-W2. Called ABB tech support and they asked me to disconnect the leads of the motor at the drive and to check voltage again because we should have any voltage with the unit in the OFF mode. ABB CASE NUMBER 7592909Performed that check and I didn’t have any voltage. I also set the VFD in HAND MODE at 60Hz and had full voltage.Electrician mentioned that on Monday when he landed the voltage wires a ground fault alarm was showing on the VFD. He checked the motor and he found a lot of debris inside the motor and also metal shavings. He used a blower to clean whatever was inside and the ground alarm disappeared. I asked him to turn the breaker off to the VFD and disconnected the wires going to the motor. Ohmed the windings of the motor and they were the same. I turned the motor by hand and it turned freely. Went to my truck and grabbed my megohmeter and tested the motor at 500Volts The megger showed that the windings are failing.Checked and tightened the connections at the motor and the ON/OFF switch before the motor. Landed the motor wires back in the VFD and tested again.Motor started operating normally. Fire alarm technician confirmed that exhaust fan was operating. From the windings reading that I got from the Megohmeter the motor should be replaced. This motor is really dirty and also needs a new belt.Job is complete.Please use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/1F08D845-8288-4192-AAC4-82C62902EF0A

ADDISON NOT PROVIDING CONSTANT DISCHARGE TEMPERATURE The Addison RTU at Vaccitech is not providing a constant discharge air temperature (DAT).  The setpoint is set at 55F and the commissioning agent noticed the DAT anywhere from 49F to 60F.  Addison recommends disabling the hot gas reheat and subcooling coil to help limiting the DAT range.  According to Edward from Addison he recommends we take the following actions:1. Put the hot gas reheat MRV1 valve in hand and reduce the voltage output to zero. UO-04. This will prevent the compressor discharge gas from going to the reheat coil.2. Put the subcooling enable hand off auto switch to off. This will turn off the subcooling.3. Set the SAT cooling and heating setpoints to 55° F.4. Set the dehumidification setpoint to a high dewpoint temperature like 90° F. This will prevent the unit from operating in dehumidification mode.Please do this and monitor for an hour to see if the DAT stays close to 55F . If possible, we recommend Jimmy Beal if available. Found an outside air louver located in the attic of the lactation room. We discovered a supply fan, located above the lactation room drop ceiling, that supplies Outside air to the indoor FCUs (fan coil units). These FCUs condition the OA and deliver the mixed conditioned air to the building.  Minimum Outside air requirements in commercial settings are necessary per local codes. 3rd party Air balancing (usually contracted by the mechanical contractor) is key to setup and verification that OA requirements designated my the Design Mechanical Engineer are met. Holes are drilled into the OA duct and Air Balancers use specific instruments to calculate airflow and utilize the manual air dampers to throttle airflow to set airflow rates. These holes are  then filled with red plastic plugs to reduce air leakage. Plugs were found at the supply fan inlet and outlet to read total airflow.  These plugs were installed in the duct insulation however no holes were drilled into the metal duct. -A second duct was tied into the louver and ducted downstairs to multiple FCUs located in and around the storage room. This duct was does not have any supply fan to force OA into the FCUs.  Instead it relies on the FCU’s fan and negative pressure to pull air into the building. It is uncommon to see both OA supply methods used together in the same building as the Supply Fans force airflow and create a positive building pressure compared to the pressure outside of the building.  If the building is always in positive pressure then the 2nd OA delivery method would, in theory, never deliver OA to the building as the building pressure would need to be less than the the pressure outside the building. -No air filter was found installed in the duct with supply fan. A 10x12x1 is required. We installed an 8x12x1 as it was the closest size available. No air filter or filter rail/rack was found in the negative pressure duct. -A supply fan and OA louver were located on in the 1st floor electrical room. This device was already discovered by and being maintained by Daniel. -OA supply ductwork has OA motorized dampers that “automatically” open and close to supply and remove OA from each FCU. Recommended loosening all Cush lamps so they slide freely and unrestrained on the rack, removal of 45° fittings, and expansion loops to be installed at every 32’ of straight horizontal piping. 10- The VRV refrigerant piping onsite was found incomplete. VRV piping must remain clean and free of debris and dust. 11- The VRV piping insulation installed is 1/2” thickness and not completely insulated. Electrical conduit is obstructing service access. The Energy Recovery Cartridges require removal and regular maintenance. A minimum of 20” of clear space needs to be provided as shown in the Daikin IOM.  This equipment is Not Serviceable. Also, needs a filter rail to be installed in the supply duct prior to the duct heater. The Exhaust duct requires a filter rail as well prior to the duct connection and Energy Recovery Cartridge. 14- The contractor was still in progress of “piping cleanup” as they claimed to had an incident where vacuum pump oil entered the VRV Piping.  Recommended submitting final piping lengths to the Sales Engineer to ensure VRV pipe sizes to not change from the original submittal. 15- Drain piping found incomplete. FCUs will produce condensate during startup. ******COMPLETE*****Shared findings with the SE. Please use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/144862D0-AA92-497C-B0E3-AD90A0304BEE

1220 L St NW AAON Unit 5/23/23Jacob EAAON Unit Exhaust Fan Not RunningArrived onsite and checked in with Luis, Engineer for CBRE. Received access to second floor AAON Ahu. Got a back story from Luis that another contractor installed a new motor that Havtech wrote up was bad. Now the new motor will not come on and run because it’s not getting a 0-10VDC signal to come on and run, according to the motor installing contractor. Went to unit and hooked up laptop to see what the unit is doing in prism. I checked the AO4 relay, which is the Exhaust fan motor signal relay, for voltage going to the exhaust fan motor. There wasn’t any voltage present at the relay. I then went through the schematic of the unit and found the PEX relay is relay Output 3. Nothing was wired up to output 3, instead the white and blue wire, which is the control wire for the Heat wheel, and the gray wire, which is for the PEX are wired together on relay output 1. I turned power off to unit and wired the outputs on the controller correctly to the wiring schematic. Turned power back onto unit and PEX still didn’t turn on. I checked building pressure thermistor and it is sending 2.5vdc back to the AI5 relay. This means the building pressure thermistor is working properly. I contacted AAON tech support to figure out the configurations for this unit. After speaking with tech support, I changed the building pressure setpoint and programmed output relay 3 for the PEX. After I did that, I have 10VDC signal coming out of the AO4 relay on controller going to the Exhaust Fan Motor. The motor still wouldn’t run, so I began troubleshooting motor and found one leg of power only had 30vac when it’s supposed to have 277vac. I turned power off to unit and traced the motor leak wires back to EF-FU1. I found that the L2 and L3 wires were wired up on the HW-FU1 which is fuse block for the heat wheel. Found 57° entering chilled water, and 43° leaving chilled water, thus indicating a lack of water flow through the evaporator. I begun tracing piping, and identifying valves were in their proper position, however the bypass valve was extremely hard to access. I called Dylan to check on our controls side as I was curious of the building differential pressure setpoint, and actual reading. Upon speaking with Dylan, he found the building differential was 38psi, and the setpoint was 15psi. He also found the bypass valve was 100% closed. I questioned why the bypass valve was closed, as he begun investigating the programming of the building bypass valve, he found the valve was programmed backwards. It was set up as reverse acting, when it needed to be direct acting. So when the building differential increased due to lack of load in the building, the valve begun to shut, when it actually needed to open to allow proper flow through the evaporator barrel on the chiller. Once Dylan corrected the programming issue, I immediately found an increase in differential pressure across the evaporator, and a huge reduction of temperature split across the evaporator. I then proceeded to check the previously installed Paddle flow switch, after making proper spring adjustments I was able to confirm the chiller closes flow switch upon flow, and opens flow switch upon the building pump stopping. I now had to remove the wiring from the incorrect differential pressure switch last installed, and run wiring back to the new paddle switch. Once it was all wired correctly I was able to confirm proper flow. Checked out with willie and explained my findings and what work I performed. Job complete. Note: All material purchased for this job was not used, I will return all materials. Please use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/30BCF98F-5701-4162-B973-BBAB27EF4928

As the discharge pressure would rise, the oil in the site glass would come down and go into a warning and then would go into alarm and turn the compressor off after about 5 minutes of running. Checked to make sure all water valves were in the proper position. Made sure the proper dampers were open. Cleared the alarm for circuit 1 and compressor 1 came on and ran. After 5 minutes, the compressor went into alarm again for low oil pressure and the site glass was almost empty of oil. Hooked up temperature probes and gauges across the liquid line solenoid valve and filter drier. Cleared alarm for circuit 1 and compressor 1 came on and ran. Found there wasn’t a temperature difference across the filter drier, so we hooked up temperature probes on both sides of the solenoid valve. Found a temperature difference across the liquid line solenoid valve for circuit 1. When there is a temperature difference across the solenoid valve, there is either a faulty valve or the solenoid coil isn’t being energized properly. We forced the unit off and turned power off to unit. Unhooked the liquid line solenoid coil and put a magnet on the valve body to see if the magnet would pull the valve open to allow refrigerant to pass through valve. Turned power on to unit and observed operation. Circuit 1 came on and we monitored pressures and temperatures across the liquid line solenoid valve. The solenoid valve is supposed to be open during unit operation and it was only opening half way allowing minimum refrigerant to pass through the valve causing the suction pressure to drop and losing the oil out of the compressor. We documented the temperature across the liquid line solenoid valve for circuit 1 during operation. Unit will need a new liquid line solenoid valve, solenoid coil, new filter drier cores, and new refrigerant. The pressures for circuit 1 look low and without having a proper liquid line solenoid valve operation, adding refrigerant to circuit 1 isn’t a good option at this time. With circuit 1 being in alarm, we began looking at circuit 2. Circuit 2 was also in alarm for low oil pressure upon arrival. We observed operation of circuit 2 once the compressor came on and ran. We tested circuit 2 in all operating modes, which include blower mode, Dehumidification, A/C, Space heat, and Pool Heat. We monitored temperatures and pressures and was not able to get circuit 2 to go into any oil pressure alarm. The only alarm that was generated for circuit 2 was low pressure alarm. That was generated by me opening the door of the unit in the evaporator section, which send the air out of the door way and not across the coil. That will bring the suction pressure down while in operation. We continued to monitor circuit 2 and it is running properly under normal operation with no alarms at this time. Circuit 1 is in alarm and will not run until alarm is cleared and the repair is made on the liquid line solenoid valve. We did find oil coming from the bottom fitting on the circuit 2 liquid line solenoid valve. I recommend replacing the solenoid valve, solenoid coil, and filter drier core for circuit 2. Also, I recommend putting new refrigerant back into circuit 2 once the new liquid line solenoid valve and filter drier cores are replaced. Once the refrigerant is recovered, there is a possibility the refrigerant charge recovered is lower than the factory charge for circuit 2 because of the leak on the liquid line solenoid valve bottom fitting. Drive had power and confirmed that was getting the correct power. Drive had a 2021 alarm saying that start enable 1 was missing. Checked and programmed the parameters. I was still getting the same alarm. Checked the wiring and noticed that one of the wires was landed incorrectly and the safety interlock was not getting close. Fixed the wiring and alarm cleared.Building engineer came back with and electrician and the fire alarm technician so we can test the system. I set the drive on hand mode and the drive was sending power but motor did run and I will get an overcurrent alarm. With the VFD in off mode I was getting 19.5VAC between U2-V2, U2-W2 and 0VAC between V2-W2. Called ABB tech support and they asked me to disconnect the leads of the motor at the drive and to check voltage again because we should have any voltage with the unit in the OFF mode. ABB CASE NUMBER 7592909Performed that check and I didn’t have any voltage. I also set the VFD in HAND MODE at 60Hz and had full voltage.Electrician mentioned that on Monday when he landed the voltage wires a ground fault alarm was showing on the VFD. He checked the motor and he found a lot of debris inside the motor and also metal shavings. He used a blower to clean whatever was inside and the ground alarm disappeared. I asked him to turn the breaker off to the VFD and disconnected the wires going to the motor. Ohmed the windings of the motor and they were the same. I turned the motor by hand and it turned freely. Went to my truck and grabbed my megohmeter and tested the motor at 500Volts The megger showed that the windings are failing.Checked and tightened the connections at the motor and the ON/OFF switch before the motor. Landed the motor wires back in the VFD and tested again.Motor started operating normally. Fire alarm technician confirmed that exhaust fan was operating. From the windings reading that I got from the Megohmeter the motor should be replaced. '- TaskSite visit to assist trouble shooting motor and vfd on DOAS -1 - Summary Arrived on site to meet Tim M and Jason from BRRJ. Once on roof I went over the symptoms of the RTU before and after the change. Found the OA filters slamm dirty from pollen and being this is a 100% OA unit these should be changes monthly if not by monthly. The date on the filters was from March when we ask them to be changed before our last visit. Jason had some on hand so I swapped them out and dated them. Tim went through and verified the motor connections, I test ran the unit and after multiple runs with the door open and closed I could run the vfd at max 75%. I found that we had good fuses and all three legs of voltage going into the vfd and leaving to the motor. The problem I found was the amp draw on line side, I only have current on L2 and L3. L1 even though it has voltage didn’t draw any amps and that would explain the input phase loss alarms I was seeing. I limited the vfd to 40 hz (71%) the vfd runs at this speed with out alarm. It’s maintaining DC bus voltage at this load but any higher it will alarm. I instructed the customer the unit could be ran if needed especially on a hot day but if he should keep it off until we know the eta of a replacement VFD to keep down the risk of damage or cost of materials if more items were to fail due to storms or operation in its limping state. The techs on Friday did a great job on the motor replacement in short notice and went just about as far as they could due to their resources with minimizing risk to the equipment and new motor. Jason told me he will shut the unit down by BAS and not the disconnect. I test ran the cooling and compressor operation due to some alarms I have no history on from the OA fan motors. The unit cycled on and off the compressor circuit and modulated with not issue or fault. - To do Submitted a quote needed XOI on a replacement vfd. - Tools used Hand tools - Materials used None Please use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/A63E7D92-32E0-4DEA-AF36-823FF82E217E

'- TaskSecond opinion on operation of H-2 humidifier- Summary Arrived on site and met with DJ. Gained access to the roof and the humidifier. I found it not in alarm and idle with no demand. DJ mentioned he had a alarm on it yesterday and the last alarm was 4/5/23 **IMW -2 = “The Ignition module identified has failed to ignite within the allotted time(4 minutes).” I jumped the unit out to start to run, changed the control signal to 0-5 vdc so I can use the internal 5 volts from the humidifier to give me a 100% demand. The humidifier went from idle to humidity and started both burners. I staged the unit up and down from 100% to 40% cycling the demand over 10 mins or so to watch it stage and start. I worked with DJ on his laptop to view the AHU and we can see the increase in RH and the status of the humidifier. I found no issue at the humidifier in its operation or response to commands. I released the 0-5 vdc control command setting back to 2-10 and removed my jumpers. * I did notice that the AHU was putting out 51 degrees DAT when it was 57 outside air temp and most of the VAVs and VNTs were in reheat and the second floor was cool in temps. There must not be a reset for DAT on VAV box demand which is abnormal in a BAS system and this mode is technically dehumidifying cooling the air and reheating at the boxes. If we were to be in a humidification demand in the space there would be not enough warm discharge air to absorb the humidity and we could see low space rh levels. The discharge of the AHU would need to be raised in a call for humidity to 60 or 65 especially when all the VAVs are needing to heat anyways. Pretty industry standard sequence. * Also noticed some VAVs and VNTs in heating and the entering air being 51 and the leaving air only a few degrees higher some in the high 50s and mid to upper 60s with three stages. The one VNT with three stages showed 88 deg so I know what a good box with three stages on looks like. The others may need to be investigated. - To do I spoke to DJ and the next time any alarms occur he will send me photos of the graphics from the AHU 1,2, and 3, the alarm from the actual humidifier and the second floor graphic showing demand to temp. We will review and try to identify what if any where the alarm is coming from or which one he is seeing. - Tools used Hand tools - Materials Used None Please use the following URL to view related photos/videos:https://vision.xoeye.io/partners/havtech/activity/2E7894D7-9FA9-42F5-A77E-546F0FD015F4
